The rally, however, came as the Treasury market showed a different signal. Seeking Alpha analyst
highlighted the growing disconnect, asking, “Does something have to give?”
Hecht noted that U.S. 30-year Treasury bond futures fell to their lowest level since 2002, reflecting elevated borrowing costs as investors reassess inflation and fiscal risks.

“Historically, rising interest rates to a nearly quarter-of-a-century high are bearish for stocks,” Hecht stated, noting that higher yields can draw capital away from equities and toward fixed income.
Yet that traditional relationship has not held, despite stubborn inflation, record U.S. debt and geopolitical uncertainty.
Hecht said markets may ultimately react with a lag, but acknowledged that “rising rates and rising stocks defy the historical status quo.”
With the November 3 U.S. midterm election also approaching, investors face another source of uncertainty.
The key question, Hecht said, is whether “a volatile storm” is ahead or markets are entering “a new paradigm in late 2026.”
